155.title: Kathina
155.hook: at the end of the rains lay people offer cloth for new robes
155.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, within a month after the rains retreat ends, lay people hold kathina ceremonies with processions and food, offering robe cloth and other necessities to the monastic community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, uposatha: a small retreat on a free day, ordinary things done slowly and awake. Your line was a retreat at home.

Thirty monks set out to see the Buddha. Forest monks from a town called Pava, planning to spend the rainy season near him at Savatthi. But the start of the rains catches them on the road, six yojanas short, as the text counts it. The rule is the rule: stay in one place. So they spend three whole months stuck at Saketa, close enough to picture him, too far to reach. When the retreat ends, they set off through rain and deep mud, and arrive soaked, robes filthy and heavy with water. What happens next, tradition says, is the root of a festival Theravada monasteries still keep after the rains.
screen: `THIRTY MONKS ON THE ROAD.` → `THE RAINS CATCH THEM.` → `THEY ARRIVE SOAKED.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook. The Buddha welcomes the thirty, asks how their retreat went, and hears about the waiting and the mud. He answers with a new allowance: at the end of the rains, monks who have kept the retreat may receive cloth and make new robes. That is the kathina. The word means firm, or hard, and tradition explains it as the wooden frame the cloth was stretched on for sewing. In the old practice, the whole community worked together, cutting, sewing and dyeing, to finish a robe in a single day. What makes it a festival? Monks aren't allowed to ask for cloth. It has to be offered. So lay people do the offering. Within a month after the rains end, in Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Cambodia, families and villages organize kathina ceremonies: processions, music, food, money trees hung with small gifts for the monastery, and at the center, a bolt of cloth. Notice who receives it. The cloth goes to the community as a whole, not to one favorite monk. The monks agree together which of them will receive it, traditionally one whose robes are most worn. The rains began with staying still; they end with giving. Three months of practice in one place, then a day of thank you, with something useful. Not money for its own sake, not a trophy: cloth, for the robe a monk wears every day.
screen: `A NEW ALLOWANCE: CLOTH FOR ROBES.` · `KATHINA — THE FIRM FRAME.` · `MONKS CAN'T ASK; IT MUST BE OFFERED.` · `GIVEN TO THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `THE RAINS END IN GIFTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has been steady for you lately, a colleague, a neighbor, a teacher, someone at home, and think about what they'd actually use: a meal, a tool, a warm pair of socks, an hour of help, a book they mentioned. Let one gift come to mind, and notice the gladness of planning it, the first of the three gladnesses you met in the giving week. Then rest with the breath.
Kathina. The robe-cloth offering at the end of the rains, named for the firm frame the cloth was stretched on.
Your line: the rains end in gifts. Something useful, never a trophy. Day one hundred fifty-five.

156.title: Camp 3 close: your practice
156.hook: a morning bow, a sitting, a walk, metta, the precepts, a gift, the holy days
156.howItsDone: Many lay Buddhists keep a simple daily rhythm, such as bowing and chanting at a home shrine in the morning, sitting or metta in the evening, the five precepts through the week, giving to the monastery, and the major holy days through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kathina: cloth offered to the whole community for new robes. Your line was the rains end in gifts. Today, the last day of camp three.

On day ninety-seven, camp three began with four short phrases: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease. Since then you've sat with sixteen steps of the breath, walked a lane of twenty paces, taken the refuges, met the five precepts, given without a receipt, bowed three times, lit a candle, kept the holy days, and learned what a retreat is. That's a lot of practice. Today it all gathers into something you can actually keep.
screen: `DAY 97: FOUR PHRASES.` → `BREATH, WALKING, PRECEPTS, GIVING.` → `NOW, SOMETHING YOU CAN KEEP.`

segments.voice: Camp three was built to add up: a morning, an evening, a week and a year. The morning, built on day one hundred forty-four: a bow, the homage, the breath, a wish of metta, and a dedication of whatever good was done. Ten minutes. The evening: metta for sleep, kindness sent out in six directions, or a short sitting of your own, with the hindrances named when they visit. The week holds the rest. A walk that's also a practice, on the lane or on the way to the bus. The five precepts, kept as trainings and taken again whenever one slips. A gift, small and wholehearted, with no receipt. And maybe, now and then, a quiet half-day at home. The year is the holy days: Vesak in May, Asalha Puja in July, the rains retreat and its three-month practice, kathina in the autumn, Magha Puja in February or March. The tradition has a pair of words for all this. Pariyatti is learning the teaching: reading, listening, studying. Patipatti is practicing it: sitting, keeping precepts, giving. Camp two was mostly stories, camp three mostly practice. Tomorrow, camp four turns to the text itself: the Dhammapada, a book of the Buddha's sayings in verse, read in order, one piece a day. The practice doesn't stop there. Each day's verse comes with a sit and a line to carry, so the words have somewhere to land. You already know how to sit. You know how to bow, walk, give, and begin again.
screen: `A MORNING, AN EVENING.` · `A WEEK: WALK, PRECEPTS, A GIFT.` · `A YEAR: THE HOLY DAYS.` · `STUDY AND PRACTICE, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `YOU CAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: With a pen, or just in your mind, sketch your week: which pieces of the morning practice you'll keep; metta, a sitting, or both in the evening; a walk, a gift and one precept somewhere in the week; one holy day in the year. Keep it realistic, not heroic. When the sketch feels right, put it down and sit with the breath, the way you've done a hundred times now.
Patipatti. Practice, the doing of the teaching: a morning, an evening, a week and a year of it, gathered into something you can keep.
Your line: you can do this. A small plan you keep beats a big one you drop. Camp three, complete.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhist practice means long hours of meditation.
what it means: a rhythm of small practices: a morning, an evening, a week and a year.
what a scholar hears: Theravada commentaries speak of pariyatti (study), patipatti (practice) and pativedha (realization) as the three parts of the true teaching.

157.title: Opening the Dhammapada
157.hook: 423 verses in 26 chapters, "the path of dhamma"; the best-loved book of the Buddha's sayings
157.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Dhammapada is memorized, chanted and taught, and some Buddhists know many of its verses by heart; teachers often give a talk on a single verse and the story the commentary tells about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, patipatti: a morning, an evening, a week and a year of practice. Your line was you can do this. Now camp four begins: the text.

If you've ever seen a Buddhist quote on a poster, a mug or a yoga studio wall, there's a fair chance it was claimed to come from one small book. Some of those quotes really are in it. Some are not in it at all. The real book is short enough to read in an afternoon, and deep enough to keep coming back to. For the next seventy-five days, you and i will read it in order, a few verses at a time, so you'll know exactly what it says.
screen: `THE QUOTE ON THE MUG.` → `SOME REAL, PLENTY NOT.` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada is four hundred twenty-three short verses in twenty-six chapters. It sits in the Pali Canon, in the part called the minor collection, but its verses are anything but minor in practice. In Theravada countries it is memorized and chanted, and some people know dozens of verses by heart. The name has two halves. Dhamma you know: the teaching, and the way things truly are. Pada has several meanings: a foot, a footstep, a path, and also a line of verse. So Dhammapada can mean the path of the dhamma, the words of the dhamma, or the verses of the dhamma, and the tradition happily hears all of them at once. Each verse is meant to be carried: short, rhythmic, easy to remember on a walk. Each chapter gathers verses around one theme, with titles like the twin verses, earnestness, thought, flowers, the fool, the wise, anger, happiness, the elephant, and thirst. An old commentary adds a story for almost every verse, telling who the Buddha was speaking to and why, and some of those stories are coming. The translation here is the one Max Müller published in 1881, in the Sacred Books of the East. His English is old-fashioned in places, and when his wording and the Pali part ways, i'll say so. Tomorrow, verse one.
screen: `423 VERSES, 26 CHAPTERS.` · `PADA — FOOT, PATH, LINE OF VERSE.` · `A STORY BEHIND ALMOST EVERY VERSE.` · `MAX MÜLLER'S ENGLISH, 1881.` · then, large: `THE PATH, IN VERSES.`

segments.voice: Here are the twenty-six chapter titles in Müller's English; just listen, and notice which one pulls at you: the twin verses, earnestness, thought, flowers, the fool, the wise man, the venerable, the thousands, evil, punishment, old age, self, the world, the Buddha, happiness, pleasure, anger, impurity, the just, the way, miscellaneous, the downward course, the elephant, thirst, the mendicant, the brahmana. Which one was yours? Hold that title gently, and let the breath take over.
Dhammapada. The path of the dhamma, or the verses of the dhamma: pada means both a step and a line.
Your line: the path, in verses. Your chapter is on its way. Day one hundred fifty-seven, done.

158.title: The mind comes first (1–2)
158.hook: all that we are is the result of what we have thought; pain follows an evil thought as the wheel follows the ox
158.howItsDone: The opening verses of the Dhammapada are among the most often chanted and memorized Buddhist verses; teachers use them to explain that intention (cetana) shapes action and its results.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Dhammapada opened: four hundred twenty-three verses, twenty-six chapters. Your line was the path, in verses. Today, verse one.

An ox cart on a dirt road in ancient India. The ox leans into the yoke and steps forward. Behind it, the heavy wooden wheel turns and follows, rut by rut, wherever the ox goes. The wheel has no say. It can't choose a different road. Everyone in the Buddha's world had watched that a thousand times. And the first verse of the Dhammapada takes that ordinary sight and says: this is how your life works.
screen: `AN OX CART ON A DIRT ROAD.` → `THE WHEEL HAS NO SAY.` → `THIS IS HOW YOUR LIFE WORKS.`

segments.voice: Here is verse one in Max Müller's English: “All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.” Verse two is its twin, the same shape with one change: if someone speaks or acts with a pure thought, “happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.” That's why chapter one is called the twin verses: the wheel and the shadow, pain and happiness, mirroring each other. Müller's opening line is famous, but the Pali is even more direct. Roughly: mind goes before all things; mind is their chief; they are made by mind. Mind comes first. Speech and action follow, and they carry the quality of the mind they came from. The old commentary tells a story for verse one. A blind monk named Cakkhupala walked up and down one night and stepped on many insects. Other monks were shocked: he'd killed living things. The Buddha said no. He didn't see them, and he didn't intend it. There was no evil thought behind the step. For this tradition, what matters is the intention an act comes from. That's why the verse starts with the mind, not the deed. This isn't a promise that thinking happy thoughts fixes everything. It's closer to a warning, and an invitation. What you set going in the mind gets pulled along behind you. And you can watch the ox before the wheel starts to turn.
screen: `VERSE ONE: THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.` · `VERSE TWO: THE SHADOW THAT STAYS.` · `THE PALI: MIND GOES BEFORE ALL.` · `THE BLIND MONK: NO INTENT, NO FAULT.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.`

segments.voice: Let the breath find its own pace, and watch for the ox: when a thought comes, a worry, a plan, a memory, notice what it does to your mood before you're carried off, a tightening chest, a softening face, a small lift or a small sinking. You don't have to change anything; just see the thought step forward and feel the wheel of your mood begin to follow. Then come back to the breath and wait for the next one.
Manopubbangama. Having mind as forerunner: the Dhammapada's first two verses, where mind goes before all, and words and deeds follow, like a wheel or a shadow.
Your line: the wheel follows the ox. Mind first; the rest follows. See you tomorrow.

159.title: "He abused me" (3–6)
159.hook: hatred never ceases by hatred, only by not-hatred; this is an old rule (Dhammapada 5)
159.howItsDone: Verse five of the Dhammapada is often recited; teachers use verses three to six to show that resentment is kept alive by rehearsing it, and ended by not answering hatred with hatred.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manopubbangama: the mind comes first, and words and deeds follow. Your line was the wheel follows the ox.

Two in the morning. Someone lies awake, replaying it. What was said at the meeting. The look on a face. The perfect answer that came too late. The scene has been turned over so often it's worn smooth, like a stone in a pocket, and it still stings each time. The Dhammapada's third verse puts that replay into a single line, as if it had been listening at the bedroom door.
screen: `2AM. REPLAYING IT.` → `A STONE WORN SMOOTH.` → `IT STILL STINGS.`

segments.voice: Verse three, in Müller's English: “‘He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,’—in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease.” Verse four is its twin: in those who don't harbor such thoughts, hatred will cease. Notice where the problem is placed. Not only in what the other person did, but in the replay. The verse doesn't say the insult didn't happen. It says hatred lives on in the harboring. Then verse five: “hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love.” Müller wrote love. The Pali word is averena: by non-hatred, by not hating back. It's quieter than love, and maybe more realistic: you don't have to feel warm toward the person, you just stop feeding the fire. The verse ends: this is an old rule. In the Pali, an eternal law: not something new, but an ancient rule. The commentary sets verse five in a story of two women whose rivalry ran on through lifetime after lifetime, each taking revenge for the last, until the Buddha stopped the cycle. Verse six belongs to a famous quarrel among the monks of Kosambi, who split over a small matter of rules. It says, roughly, that people forget everyone comes to an end here, and those who remember it let their quarrels settle. So chapter one gives two tools for the 2am replay: notice that the hatred lives in the harboring, and remember how short all of this is.
screen: `VERSE THREE: THE REPLAY.` · `HATRED LIVES IN THE HARBORING.` · `VERSE FIVE: BY NOT HATING BACK.` · `REMEMBER HOW SHORT THIS IS.` · then, large: `HATRED ENDS BY NOT-HATRED.`

segments.voice: Let a small old grudge come to mind, not the biggest, a mild one, and hear its sentence once, your own version of “he abused me, he robbed me.” Instead of replaying it, feel what it does in the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach, and breathe into that place. You don't have to forgive anyone right now; just try not feeding it for the length of this sit, and when the replay starts again, come back to the breath.
Averena. By non-hatred: the old rule, in verses three to six, that only not-hatred ends the thought “he abused me” that keeps hatred alive.
Your line: hatred ends by not-hatred. The stone in the pocket can rest. That's day one hundred fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 159 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WIND AND THE ROCK.`

160.title: The wind and the rock (7–14)
160.hook: Mara overthrows the careless like wind a weak tree, not the steady; rain gets through a badly thatched roof
160.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the thatched-roof verses to explain guarding the senses and steady daily practice: small, repeated repairs rather than one great effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, averena: by not hating back, the old rule for the replay that keeps hatred alive. Your line was hatred ends by not-hatred.

After a big storm, walk through a neighborhood and look at what came down. Often it isn't the tallest tree. It's the one that was already hollow, or shallow-rooted, or leaning. The old oak at the corner is still standing; the young tree with no roots is across the road. Inside the houses, the leaks show up exactly where the roof was already weak: the missing shingle, the cracked flashing you meant to fix in the summer. Storms don't make weak spots. They find them.
screen: `AFTER THE STORM.` → `THE HOLLOW TREE FALLS.` → `STORMS FIND WEAK SPOTS.`

segments.voice: Verse seven describes someone living for pleasure only, senses unguarded, eating without limit, idle and weak. And Mara, the tempter, the figure who stands for everything that pulls people off the path, “will certainly overthrow him, as the wind throws down a weak tree.” Verse eight is the twin: the one who lives with guarded senses, moderate in food, faithful and strong, Mara can no more throw down “than the wind throws down a rocky mountain.” Wind and rock. The wind is the same for both. What differs is what it meets. Verses nine to twelve warn against wearing the robe without the inner change, and against mistaking what's false for what's true. Then thirteen and fourteen: “As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind.” And the twin: “As rain does not break through a well-thatched house, passion will not break through a well-reflecting mind.” The commentary tells these verses about Nanda, the Buddha's own half-brother. He became a monk on the day of his wedding, almost without meaning to, and pined for the bride he'd left behind. His roof leaked everywhere. But with patience and practice, the story says, he thatched it, and became known for guarding his senses. Thatching isn't done once. You check it before the rains, replace a bundle here, tie down a corner there. Not an unbreakable fortress: a roof kept in repair.
screen: `VERSE SEVEN: THE WEAK TREE.` · `VERSE EIGHT: THE ROCKY MOUNTAIN.` · `THIRTEEN: RAIN THROUGH BAD THATCH.` · `NANDA, WHO THATCHED HIS ROOF.` · then, large: `THATCH THE ROOF.`

segments.voice: Like someone walking around a house before the rains, look over your own roof: where does the weather get in? Maybe the phone at night, hunger, tiredness, or one particular person who always gets under your skin; don't judge it, just find one weak spot and see it clearly. Then ask, quietly, what one bundle of thatch could go there, an earlier bedtime, a snack before the hard meeting, and rest with that.
Ducchanna. Badly thatched: the same rain that leaks through a bad roof passes over a good one, as the same wind throws down a weak tree, not a mountain.
Your line: thatch the roof. A bundle at a time, before the rains. Day one hundred sixty, done.

161.title: Other people's cows (15–20)
161.hook: one who recites much but doesn't act is like a cowherd counting others' cows (Dhammapada 19)
161.howItsDone: Theravada teachers pair study with practice, and some cite the cowherd verse to warn that reciting scripture is not the same as living it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ducchanna: badly thatched, the wind and the rock. Your line was thatch the roof. Today, the end of the week and the end of chapter one.

A hired cowherd stands at the gate at the end of the day, counting cattle as they come in. Thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three. He knows every animal: which cow gives the most milk, which calf was born last spring. But at the end of the season, not one drop of that milk is his. He's counting other people's cows. The Dhammapada uses that picture for a very particular kind of person, someone who might be a lot like you and me, a few weeks into reading a book of wisdom.
screen: `A COWHERD AT THE GATE.` → `HE KNOWS EVERY ANIMAL.` → `NOT ONE DROP IS HIS.`

segments.voice: The chapter ends with three more twin pairs. Verses fifteen and sixteen: the one who does evil “mourns in this world, and he mourns in the next”; the one who does good delights in both. Seventeen and eighteen say the same with suffering and happiness. Then nineteen and twenty, the cowherd. Verse nineteen, in Müller's English: “The thoughtless man, even if he can recite a large portion (of the law), but is not a doer of it, has no share in the priesthood, but is like a cowherd counting the cows of others.” Priesthood is Müller's word; the Pali means something like a share in the life of a seeker. Verse twenty is the twin: someone who can recite only a little, but lets go of greed, hatred and delusion and lives it, has that share in full. The commentary tells it about two friends who became monks together. One studied the scriptures and had many students. The other learned only a little, went off to the forest, meditated, and became fully awakened. When the scholar came to test his friend with hard questions, the Buddha asked them both about the deeper stages of the path, and only the quiet one could answer. So look back at chapter one. The mind comes first, manopubbangama. Hatred ends by not-hatred. Thatch the roof. And now: none of it is yours by being counted. Knowing verses is fine; it's what these lessons are made of. But the verse you live today outweighs the ten you can recite.

segments.voice: Let chapter one's four lines pass by once, like cattle through a gate: the wheel follows the ox, hatred ends by not-hatred, thatch the roof, not someone else's cows. Choose just one, not the one that sounds wisest but the one you could actually live in the life you have, and hold it for a few breaths, picturing one moment later today when you might use it. Then let it go and rest with the breath.
Other people's cows. Knowing many verses without living them is counting cattle that aren't yours; living a few makes them your own.
Your line: not someone else's cows. Chapter one, all the way through. That's day one hundred sixty-one.
